questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go somewhere where the society was different from what I was used to at home in Denmark, and which also offered good educational and career opportunities. San Francisco in the US seemed to be the perfect place to pursue these goals.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: San Francisco was everything I had dreamed of. However, be aware that since the society is so different from what you're used to back home, it may require a period of adjustment before you feel comfortable in it.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was very easy. The University of Copenhagen as well as the university in San Francisco, UC Law SF, had good guides and if I had any questions, I could contact them.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We had an introduction day before the semester started, where we were presented with everything we needed and were given contact information for all the relevant people.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Initially, we were given a lot of information and it seemed like we could easily contact them and get further information. However, it was relatively difficult to get answers to questions from them afterwards. I experienced several times that I was ignored.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
The university offers you the opportunity to live in their dormitory. However, this dormitory is very expensive. Prices start from 16,000 DKK. In addition, the dormitory (and even university) is located in the area where most homeless and criminal people live. The university had provided security, but in any case, it was not the safest place to live. 

I therefore chose to find something else. This was relatively difficult. I ended up finding an apartment on Airbnb and making an agreement with the landlord outside of Airbnb.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: San Francisco is a really beautiful city. So all the neighborhoods are really nice to live in, except downtown (where the university and the dorm are located). However, be aware that if you're planning on having late nights at the university, it can be a bit unsafe coming home, as you'll have to pass through the homeless neighborhood first.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The dorm is really nice, but also really expensive. I wish it had been cheaper.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The university tried to make it as easy to understand as possible, but there were so many things to answer and go through, which made it confusing.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You must first send a motivated application. If this is accepted (in all likelihood it will be, as it is only formal that you have to send a motivated application), then you need to apply for a visa. In the visa process, you must first prove to the university that you have sufficient funds to complete your stay. When I went on exchange, the amount was 130,000 DKK. If you can prove this, the university will give you an application form to apply for a visa. (The visa process is long). If you get the visa, then you need to get ready to be a student at the university, where you need to send a picture for your student card, fill out some information, and pay for student fees.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Guides and the possibility to contact the university.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I went in the spring. Around November it was possible to choose courses. They have an online portal where you can see how many places are available and sign up for the course if you want to. So you don't send an application about which courses you want and wait for a response. You have the option to change courses right up until the 2nd week of the semester. In the first week of the semester, you can try out the courses you've chosen and see if it's for you, and if not, switch to another class.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Take it easy. You'll get in and do well. Everyone else has done it, so you can too. As for the courses, you will most likely end up getting the courses you want, so just wait for someone to unsubscribe from the course you want.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The courses and teachers were good. If I had to put my finger on something, it would be that they do not have many subjects that are internationally oriented. Many of them only deal with American law, which we can't use for much afterwards.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level is neither lower nor higher than in Denmark.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It's a lot of dialog rather than monologue. The teachers expect you to be much more prepared for the classes than in Denmark, so that you can participate actively, possibly by forcing you, as they cold-call you - it's not as bad as it may sound.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: I had Criminal Law, Negotiation, Entertainment Law, and Statutory: Intellectual Property.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would definitely recommend the courses that I have taken. I don't know much about the other courses, so I can't comment on them.

Personal spending DKK per month *

Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Although it's free to study at the school, you will have to pay 5000 DKK in tuition fees. 

In addition, the university requires you to use their insurance, which costs 25,000 DKK. You can apply to use your own insurance instead. You'll most likely be rejected the first few times, after which you can contact the university (and not the insurance company) and ask them to help you. I just used Gouda.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Everything is much more expensive in the US. Even when you just go to the supermarket, a packet of butter costs at least 3-4 times the price in Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They have a lot of clubs, but no sporting activities. They don't have their own turf.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: No sporting activities... They had a lot of clubs for people who come from certain places or follow certain beliefs, for example, a club for people from the Middle East, a club for Asians. On top of that, they had associations for people with similar interests, for example, an association for people who like gaming.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend finding a club that's right for you. There is no one club that all people like. You need to find the club that you can reflect yourself in. Clubs are great for meeting new people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
In San Francisco I would recommend seeing the Golden Gate Bridge, Alcatraz, Exploratorium, China Town, Golden Gate Park, see a baseball game, see a basketball game. Hit the club on Monroe or Westwood and have a beer at Vesuvio Cafe. Relax in Golden Gate Park or Salesforce park. Go shopping on Haight Street. Mexican food in the Mission District. Sushi in Japan Town. Play tennis at Lafayette Park. 

Close to San Francisco I would recommend going to Big Sur (great nature), Yosemite National Park (great nature), Monterey (small cozy town), Santa Cruz (cool surfer town). Silicon Valley and see the headquarters of some of the world's biggest companies such as Apple and Google, or experience NASA or Stanford university. I wouldn't recommend Oakland (lots of crime) (but go if you want to see Berkeley University, which is relatively close to Oakland) and Sacramento (boring city with no life).

Places you can travel to I would recommend Los Angeles, Las Vegas (flights are only $100 round trip!!!) and Hawaii. If you have a little more money to spend, I'd recommend heading to the East Coast, specifically Miami (especially on Spring Break)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The culture was different, but since it was the same language and Americans are sweet people, it was relatively easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join some university clubs. Sign up for some sport. Go out to a club or bar. Go to Sjømannskirken, which is a Norwegian church but is a meeting point for all Scandinavians.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: They don't party until 5 am. All clubs and bars close at 2 am.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How open and welcoming Americans are.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Try to get out of your comfort zone and talk to people who are not from Denmark (if there are any), have fun, spend money like there is no tomorrow

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I think I've said everything I needed to say.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people I met and the experiences I had.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: That you knew it was all temporary.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
